opus-5.5.text:
I think the most exciting thing about Reachy Mini is that it flips the usual order of how people think about consumer robotics. Most people imagine the end state first, the humanoid that folds your laundry and does the dishes, and then they work backwards. And that's a very long road, with a lot of hardware cost and a lot of safety questions along the way. What we wanted with Reachy Mini was something you can actually put on your desk today, at a price that a hobbyist, a student, or a developer can afford, and start building with immediately.

It's small, it's expressive, it has a head that moves, antennas, a camera, microphones, a speaker, so it can look at you, listen, react. It doesn't manipulate objects in the world yet, and that's deliberate. Before robots are useful for physical tasks in the home, I think they'll be useful as an embodied interface to AI. People are already talking to models all day long, and there's something very different about talking to a thing that turns its head toward you, that looks curious, that has a presence in the room. That's a new kind of interaction, and nobody really knows yet what the killer apps are.

And that's the open-source bet, really. We don't think we, at Hugging Face, are going to come up with the best application. We think the community will. It's what we saw with models on the Hub: you put a good base out there, you make it hackable, you make sharing easy, and thousands of people build things you'd never have imagined. So Reachy Mini is fully open, the software, the SDK, the designs, and apps can be shared on the Hub like a model or a Space. Someone builds a language tutor, someone builds a game for kids, someone builds a meeting assistant that actually looks at who's speaking, and everyone else can install it in one click.

So I see it a bit like the early personal computer moment, or the early days of the Raspberry Pi. The first wave isn't mass-market consumers, it's builders. But builders are how you discover what consumers actually want. And if we get thousands of these robots out in the world, with people experimenting and sharing, we'll also collect a lot of understanding, and hopefully open data, about how humans want to live with robots. That's the foundation you need before the bigger, more capable home robots can really make sense.

r001.rationale: The response says Reachy Mini is deliberately not designed for physical tasks yet, but does not say earlier consumer robots lost appeal because they exhausted a small, fixed set of behaviors.

r002.rationale: It describes community-created apps and behaviors shared on the Hub, with examples and one-click installation, which conveys a shared app ecosystem for the robot.

r003.rationale: It argues that thousands of robots in the world would enable people to experiment and share, and points to community-built work on the Hub as a precedent for that ecosystem succeeding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about Reachy Mini is that it's really our attempt to do for robotics what we did for NLP with the Transformers library, which is to lower the barrier to entry so much that a huge community can start building on it.

If you look at where robotics is today, it feels a lot like language models in 2018 or 2019. The big labs are doing impressive things, but everything is closed, the hardware is expensive, and if you're a student or an independent developer you basically can't participate. We wanted a robot that costs a few hundred dollars, that you can assemble yourself, that's fully open source in hardware and software, and that you can program in Python in a few minutes. That's Reachy Mini.

And the consumer angle is interesting because I don't think the first killer app for home robots is going to be a humanoid folding your laundry. That's a very hard problem and it's going to take years. What I think comes much sooner is something more like a companion, an expressive little device on your desk that can see you, talk to you, react to you, and connect to all the AI models that are already very good. The LLMs and the speech models and vision models are there. What's missing is a body for them, and the body doesn't need to be a full humanoid to be useful and delightful.

So Reachy Mini is cute on purpose. It has the head, the antennas, it can look at you, it can express something. People form attachments to it very quickly, which is something we saw even with early prototypes. And then because it's open, people are building things we never anticipated. Someone makes it a chess coach, someone makes it a language tutor for their kids, someone hooks it up to their smart home. That's the kind of long tail you only get when you give the platform away rather than trying to control every use case.

The bet is that the winning consumer robotics platform will look more like the smartphone app ecosystem than like a single closed product from one company. We want to be the open layer that the whole community builds on, and Reachy Mini is the first concrete step in that direction.

r001.rationale: The response does not say earlier consumer robots lost appeal because they exhausted a small, fixed set of behaviors.

r002.rationale: It describes an open platform where the community builds unexpected uses and compares the winning platform to the smartphone app ecosystem.

r003.rationale: It says a large community can build on Reachy Mini, but does not identify rapid community growth as a reason the behavior ecosystem could succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is making robotics something people can actually experiment with at home. A small robot gives you a very different relationship with AI than a chat window. It can be present in your space, and you can explore what movement and interaction add to the experience.

But I would distinguish that potential from having a finished consumer use case. What will people want it to do every day? That’s still a question. For me, the promise of Reachy Mini as a platform is that you can let lots of people explore that question—developers, hobbyists, people who have an idea we haven’t thought of. The platform becomes really interesting when those experiments turn into experiences other people want to use.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention earlier consumer robots losing appeal or attribute that to exhausting a small, fixed set of behaviors.

r002.rationale: It describes developers and hobbyists exploring ideas, but does not clearly propose a community-created ecosystem of robot behaviors or compare it to the iPhone app ecosystem.

r003.rationale: The response does not say the Reachy Mini community is growing rapidly or identify that growth as a reason the ecosystem could succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about Reachy Mini is that it gives people a platform to experiment with what a robot in everyday life could actually be useful for. We tend to jump straight to a robot that does all the household chores, but there’s a lot to explore before that: how it interacts with you, how it understands its surroundings, and what makes you want to keep using it.

And I don’t think one team is going to discover all those applications. If you make the platform accessible and let a community build on it, people can try things you wouldn’t have imagined. The potential is really in that experimentation—going from a compelling demo to something people genuinely find useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exploring useful applications, but does not say earlier consumer robots lost appeal because they had a small, fixed repertoire of behaviors.

r002.rationale: It says a community could build on the platform, but does not describe an ecosystem of robot behaviors analogous to the iPhone app ecosystem.

r003.rationale: The response mentions a community, but does not identify rapid community growth as a reason the behavior ecosystem could succeed.
